title: Why Boats Float
learning_objectives: Explain in simple terms why a heavy steel ship floats while a small stone sinks
Use the words hull, displace and hollow in context

factual_claims.claim: An object floats if it weighs less than the water it pushes aside (displaces).
factual_claims.source: Britannica Kids, 'Buoyancy'; Science Museum Group Learning, 'Floating and sinking'

factual_claims.claim: A ball of modelling clay sinks, but the same clay shaped into a bowl floats because the bowl pushes aside more water.
Steel ships float because their hulls are hollow and full of air, so the whole ship is lighter than the water it displaces.
factual_claims.source: Britannica Kids, 'Ship' / 'Buoyancy'; BBC Bitesize KS2 'Why do things float?'

factual_claims.claim: Loading a boat makes it sit lower in the water; too much load and it sinks.
factual_claims.source: Science Museum Group Learning, 'Floating and sinking'

factual_claims.claim: The upward push of water on an object is called upthrust (or buoyancy).

parent_prompts: Before: a stone sinks and a huge ship floats. What is the ship made of? Then why does it float?
Try it: a ball of clay or foil, then the same piece shaped as a bowl, in a basin of water.
After: what does 'push aside' mean here? Can the child show it with their hands in the water?

pages.text: Drop a stone in a pond and it sinks. Yet a steel ship, heavier than a thousand stones, sails across the sea. How can that be?
pages.illustration_brief: A small stone sinking with a plop on the left; a large grey ship on the sea on the right.
pages.audio_script: Drop a stone in a pond and it sinks. Yet a steel ship, heavier than a thousand stones, sails across the sea. How can that be?
pages.image_alt: A stone sinking in a pond beside a large steel ship sailing on the sea.

pages.text: When you put something in water, it pushes some water out of the way. Get into a full bath and water spills over the edge. That pushed-away water is the secret.
pages.illustration_brief: A bathtub with a child stepping in; water sloshing over the rim onto the floor.
pages.audio_script: When you put something in water, it pushes some water out of the way. Get into a full bath and water spills over the edge. That pushed-away water is the secret.

vocabulary.definition: To push something out of the place it was in.
vocabulary.example: Your body displaces water when you get in the bath.

pages.image_alt: A child stepping into a full bath as water spills over the edge.

pages.text: The water pushes back up on the object. Here is the rule: if the object weighs less than the water it pushed aside, it floats. If it weighs more, it sinks.
pages.illustration_brief: Diagram: an object in water with a big upward arrow labelled by an up-arrow symbol only, and a downward arrow for weight.
pages.audio_script: The water pushes back up on the object. Here is the rule: if the object weighs less than the water it pushed aside, it floats. If it weighs more, it sinks.

vocabulary.definition: The upward push that water gives to things in it.

pages.image_alt: A tank of water with an object inside and arrows showing water pushing upward beneath it.

pages.text: A stone is small but heavy. It pushes aside only a little water, and it weighs more than that little bit. Down it goes.
pages.illustration_brief: Cross-section: a stone under water with a tiny displaced-water outline around it.
pages.audio_script: A stone is small but heavy. It pushes aside only a little water, and it weighs more than that little bit. Down it goes.
pages.image_alt: A tank with a small stone sinking to the bottom, only a little water pushed aside.

pages.text: Now take a lump of clay and roll it into a ball. It sinks, just like the stone. Flatten the same lump into a bowl shape and set it down gently. It floats!
pages.illustration_brief: Two panels: a clay ball at the bottom of a basin; the same clay as a wide bowl floating on top.
pages.audio_script: Now take a lump of clay and roll it into a ball. It sinks, just like the stone. Flatten the same lump into a bowl shape and set it down gently. It floats!
pages.image_alt: Two tanks: a clay ball on the bottom of one and a clay bowl floating in the other.

pages.text: Same clay, same weight. What changed? The bowl is wide and hollow. It pushes aside far more water than the ball did, and now that water weighs more than the clay.
pages.illustration_brief: The clay bowl floating with a large displaced-water outline compared to the small one for the ball.
pages.audio_script: Same clay, same weight. What changed? The bowl is wide and hollow. It pushes aside far more water than the ball did, and now that water weighs more than the clay.
pages.image_alt: A wide hollow clay bowl floating with many blue arrows pushing up beneath it.

pages.text: A ship is a giant clay bowl. Its body, the hull, is a huge hollow shell full of air, rooms and empty space. All that steel plus all that air still weighs less than the sea it pushes aside.
pages.illustration_brief: Cross-section of a ship's hull showing large empty spaces and decks inside; sea level marked on the outside.
pages.audio_script: A ship is a giant clay bowl. Its body, the hull, is a huge hollow shell full of air, rooms and empty space. All that steel plus all that air still weighs less than the sea it pushes aside.

vocabulary.definition: The main body of a boat or ship, the part that sits in the water.
vocabulary.example: The hull was painted red below the water line.

pages.image_alt: A cut-away ship hull showing rooms and empty air space above the waterline.

pages.text: Load a ship with boxes and it sits lower, pushing aside more water to hold the extra weight. Load it too much, so that it weighs more than the water it can push aside, and even a ship will sink.
pages.illustration_brief: Three ships side by side: empty riding high, loaded riding low, overloaded with the deck at the water line.
pages.audio_script: Load a ship with boxes and it sits lower, pushing aside more water to hold the extra weight. Load it too much, so that it weighs more than the water it can push aside, and even a ship will sink.
pages.image_alt: A ship stacked with boxes sitting low in the water; a second ship tipped and sinking.

pages.text: So the stone and the ship follow the same rule. It is not about how heavy something is. It is about how heavy it is compared with the water it pushes out of the way.
pages.illustration_brief: The stone and the ship again, now each with its displaced-water outline drawn to scale.
pages.audio_script: So the stone and the ship follow the same rule. It is not about how heavy something is. It is about how heavy it is compared with the water it pushes out of the way.
pages.image_alt: A balance scale weighing an object against the water it pushed aside.

quiz.prompt: What is the rule for floating?

options.text: It floats if it weighs less than the water it pushes aside
It floats if it is lighter than a stone
It floats if it is flat

quiz.explanation: Page 3 states the rule: if the object weighs less than the water it pushed aside, it floats.

quiz.prompt: Why does the clay bowl float when the clay ball sank?

options.text: The bowl pushes aside far more water

quiz.explanation: Page 6: same clay, same weight; the bowl pushes aside far more water than the ball did.

options.text: The main body of a ship that sits in the water

quiz.explanation: Page 7: Its body, the hull, is a huge hollow shell.

quiz.prompt: Why does a loaded ship sit lower in the water?

options.text: It must push aside more water to hold the extra weight

quiz.explanation: Page 8: it sits lower, pushing aside more water to hold the extra weight.

quiz.prompt: What is the main idea of this book?

options.text: Floating depends on weight compared with the water pushed aside, not weight alone

quiz.explanation: Page 3 gives the rule and page 9 repeats it: not how heavy, but how heavy compared with the water pushed out of the way.

quiz.prompt: Explain to a grown-up why a steel ship floats but a stone sinks. Try to use hollow and push aside.
quiz.rubric: not yet: says ships are big; with support: mentions air or hollow, with prompting; independent: the hollow hull pushes aside a lot of water, more than the ship weighs, while a stone pushes aside less than its own weight
quiz.explanation: Getting the comparison right is the whole concept; listen for weight versus displaced water, not just 'air'.

activities.prompt: Put the clay experiment in order.

items.text: Roll the clay into a ball; it sinks.
Flatten it into a bowl; it floats.
The bowl pushes aside more water.
A ship is a giant clay bowl.

activities.prompt: Match the word to its meaning.

activities.claim: Even a ship can sink if it is loaded too much.

off_screen_prompt: Make a foil ball and a foil boat from two equal pieces of kitchen foil. Float them in a bowl. Add coins to the boat one at a time and count how many it holds before it sinks.
